Sale of a child means the transfer of a child “by any person or group of persons to another for remuneration or any other consideration". 

- Child labor. Information related to employment of children in any form of work that is likely to be hazardous or to interfere with a child's education or deprives children of their childhood, their potential and their dignity, and that is harmful to physical, psychological, emotional, spiritual, moral or social development. It refers to work that:
a) Is done by children under the age of 15. The International Labour Organization (ILO) defines child labor as work that is done by children under the age of 15, but in some countries, the minimum age for employment may be higher, such as 16 or 18 years old.
b) And/or is psychologically, emotionally, physically, socially or morally dangerous and harmful to children, such as:     
o   Slavery. Information related to all forms of slavery or practices similar to slavery, such as the sale and trafficking of children, debt bondage and serfdom and forced or compulsory labor, including forced or compulsory recruitment of children for use in armed conflict,
o   Child prostitution. Information related to the use, procuring or offering of a child for prostitution, for the production of pornography or for pornographic performances,
o   Illicit activities. Information related to the use, procuring or offering of a child for illicit activities,
o  Hazardous work. Information related to: work which exposes children to physical, psychological or sexual abuse; work underground, under water, at dangerous heights or in confined spaces; work with dangerous machinery, equipment and tools, or which involves the manual handling or transport of heavy loads; work in an unhealthy environment which may, for example, expose children to hazardous substances, agents or processes, or to temperatures, noise levels, or vibrations harmfull to their health; work under particularly difficult conditions such as work for long hours or during the night or work where the child is unreasonably confined to the premises of the employer,
Work that interferes with children’s schooling. Information related to work situations that  deprive children from the opportunity to attend school; oblige them to leave school prematurely; or require them to attempt to combine school attendance with excessively long and heavy work,
Child mendicity. Information related to any act of children begging or soliciting for money, food, or other forms of support in the streets. It is a form of child labor and exploitation when children are forced or compelled to beg by either their parents, guardians, or sometimes even traffickers who exploit them for financial gain. 

- Child marriage. Information related to any formal or informal union between a person under the age of 18 with an adult or another child. It is always considered as a form of forced marriage because of the impossibility for a child to give full, free and informed consent. Forced marriage is a marriage in which one or more of the parties is married without their consent or against their will.

- Female genital mutilation (FGM) before the age of 18. Information related to all procedures involving partial or total removal of under 18 years old female external genitalia, or any other injury to an under 18 years old female genital organs for non-medical reasons.

- Violence against children. Information related to physical, psychological/emotional or sexual violence against children, including:
a) Verbal and physical violence. Information related to verbal and physical violence can take many forms, including bullying, corporal punishment, and psychological/emotional abuse.
b) Violence at school. Information related to physical violence, verbal abuse, peer-to-peer violence in and around school, bullying, sexual harassment, and corporal punishment.
c) Violence online. Information related to violence online can take many forms, including cyberbullying, sexual exploitation, exposure to hate speech and violent content (including messages that incite self-harm and even suicide), threat of online sexual exploitation and abuse.
d) Gender based violence. Information related to any harmful act or practice that is directed against a child based on their gender or perceived gender. It includes physical, sexual, and psychological/emotional violence, such as: intimate partner violence, sexual violence, child marriage, female genital mutilation, children being trafficked for sexual exploitation, female infanticide, and the so-called ‘‘honour’’ crimes.
e) Sexual violence. Information related to any sexual act, attempt to obtain a sexual act, unwanted sexual comments or advances, or acts to traffic or otherwise exploit children's sexuality using coercion, threats, or force. It includes: conflict-related sexual violence, intimate partner violence, and child trafficking for sexual exploitation.

- Children recruited by or associated with armed forces or groups. Information related to any recruitment or conscription, whether forced or voluntary, of children into any kind of regular or irregular armed force or group in any capacity, and used by parties to conflict. Warring parties use children not only as fighters, but as scouts, cooks, porters, guards, messengers and more. It includes: abduction, threat, coercion or manipulation, deprivation of nutrition and healthy living conditions, being subjected to substance abuse, etc., by armed actors.

- Migrant and displaced children. Information related to children on the move exposed to danger, detention, deprivation and discrimination/exclusion on their journeys at destination or upon return.

- Children incapacitated, injured or killed by Explosive Ordnance (EO) or exposed to harm caused by EO hazards and hazardous areas. Children are particularly vulnerable as they can be attracted to Mine, UXOs and IEDs due to their colorful appearance and because they are unaware of how dangerous they are. Some of these weapons are familiar household objects that have been turned into explosives.

- Separation from family. Information related to children separated from parents, caregivers, or relatives. Separated children are those separated from both parents, or from their previous legal or customary primary caregiver, but not necessarily from other relatives. Unaccompanied children are children who have been separated from both parents, primary caregivers and other relatives, and are not under the care of an adult who, by law or costume, is responsible for doing so.

- Children growing in alternative care. Information related to children without parental care and placed in the care of individuals or institutions other than their parents or primary caregivers (e.g., foster care, residential care, institutions, orphanage, or adoption).

- Sexual exploitation and abuse against children perpetrated by aid workers. It includes:
a) Sexual exploitation. Information related to any actual or attempted abuse of a position of vulnerability, differential power, or trust, for sexual purposes, perpetrated by aid workers against the children they serve.
b) Sexual abuse. Information related to actual or threatened physical intrusion of a sexual nature, whether by force or under unequal or coercive conditions, perpetrated by aid workers against the children they serve.

- Children deprived of legal documentation. Information related to children deprived of a legal document (birth certificate, legal identity document, etc.) that provides proof of the child's identity and nationality.

- Children deprived of their liberty by enforcement officials (such as police, military, or prison personnel). Information related to children detained or imprisoned, including in pretrial detention, correctional facilities, adult prison, or military detention centers.

- Children deprived of education and drop-out of school. Information related to children unable to access quality education, or children/adolescents that stop attending school before completing their education.

- Early pregnancy. Information related to pregnancies that occur before the age of 18.

- Forced pregnancy before the age of 18. Information related to situations where girls under the age of 18 are coerced or forced to become pregnant against their will.

- Child neglect. Information related to the failure of parents or caregivers to provide children with the basic needs for survival, including adequate food, shelter, clothing, and medical care, as well as psychological/emotional support and protection from harm. Child neglect can take many forms, including physical neglect,  psychological/emotional neglect, and educational neglect. Physical neglect involves the failure to provide adequate food, clothing, shelter, or medical care, while psychological/emotional neglect involves the failure to provide adequate psychological/emotional support and attention. Educational neglect involves the failure to provide access to education or support for children's learning and development.

- Children witnessing violence, experiencing terror, and dealing with uncertainty and anxiety.

- Female infanticide. Information on the deliberate killing of female children to be born or newborn female children because of their gender.
nodes.question: What forms of violence, neglect, exploitation, trafficking, harmful practices, and family separation are affecting children, and how do detention, schooling barriers, explosive harm, and caregiver abuse compound their protection risks?

nodes.name: Child Labor and Exploitation
nodes.definition: Information related to work by persons under 18 that is hazardous, age-inappropriate, or displaces schooling and healthy development, including slavery-like practices, debt bondage, commercial sexual exploitation (prostitution and pornography), use in illicit activities, hazardous industrial or agricultural tasks, and child mendicity.
nodes.question: Which hazardous or exploitative forms of child work—including mendicity, illicit activities, and commercial sexual exploitation—are reported, and how do they affect school attendance and development?

nodes.name: Detention Schooling Barriers and Explosive Harm
nodes.l3: Detention Schooling Barriers and Explosive Harm
nodes.definition: Information related to children deprived of liberty through detention or other confinement; children without civil or identity papers; barriers that keep children out of school; and death or injury of children from mines, unexploded ordnance, IEDs, or other explosive devices.
nodes.question: Which children are deprived of liberty, lack identity papers, remain out of school, or are killed or injured by explosive devices, and with what protection consequences?

nodes.name: Family Separation and Alternative Care
nodes.definition: Information related to unaccompanied or separated children among displaced, migrant, or crisis-affected populations, and to care arrangements outside the parental household—kinship, foster, institutional, or informal care—when parental or caregiver protection is lost or weak.
nodes.question: How many children are separated, unaccompanied, or in alternative care, and what risks arise when caregiver protection is absent or inadequate?

nodes.name: Harmful Practices and Adolescent Pregnancy
nodes.definition: Information related to child marriage, female genital mutilation or cutting before adulthood, early or forced pregnancy among girls under 18, and female infanticide, as practices causing physical, psychological, or developmental harm.

nodes.name: Documentation
nodes.definition:
Information related to all measures, acts and practices that prevent people from accessing documentation. It includes the information related to the status of the persons (e.g., statelessness) and the status of the documents, such as being lost (it can be difficult or impossible to reconstruct the information they contain), being stolen (there is a potential for identity theft or fraud), being contested (the authenticity or validity of a document is disputed, e.g., existence of multiple versions of a document, disagreement over the terms or conditions outlined in a document), being withheld (it can make it difficult to prove the eligibility for benefits or compensation) or being destroyed. Documentation can be related to the legal identity, the civil status, the statelessness status, the legal status, the immigration status, the registration documents, the recognition of diplomas and validation of certificates, and other legal documents.

- Legal identity. Refers to a person's recognized existence as a legal entity under the law. It is typically established through the issuance of a legal identity document, by State and NSAGs, such as a birth registration/certificate, ID card/identity paper, passport, which confirms a person's identity and provides proof of their legal existence. Denial of access to legal identity refers to all situations preventing a person to possess legal identity or any other fundamental documentation to be recognized as a person before the law. Legal identity is fundamental to enabling an individual to claim other rights and to enjoy fundamental entitlements, including the right to a nationality, freedom of movement, legal remedies, judicial mechanisms, due processes, etc. A lack of legal identity or civil documents puts people at increased risk of arbitrary arrest/detention, exploitation, community stigmatization, isolation, exclusion, and statelessness. 

- Civil status. Refers to the legal recognition of an individual's personal and family situation. It includes all information related to civil status documentation and certificates about birth, gender identity, marital status (single, married, divorced, partnership, etc.), relationships with family members (whether they have children or not), criminal records, and death. Those documents serve as a legal record of an individual's personal and family situation, and are often used to determine rights and obligations, such as inheritance, child custody, and property ownership. They are also required for a wide range of legal and administrative procedures, such as obtaining a passport, enrolling in school, or registering for social security benefits.

- Statelessness status. Refers to individuals that do not have a legally recognized nationality or citizenship. There are many reasons why individuals are/become stateless, including discrimination, displacement, administrative barriers, conflicts between States, being born from stateless parents, never having been registered at birth, being unable to prove nationality because of the lost/lack of documents such as birth certificate or ID card/identity paper/passport, etc.

- Legal status. Refers to a person's standing in relation to the law. It describes whether a person is legally recognized as a citizen or not, and whether they have legal rights and obligations. This can include things like their ability to enter into contracts, their right to own property, access legal remedies, and their ability to vote. Legal status can also refer to a person's status in relation to specific laws or legal systems, such as their immigration status, criminal record, or marital status.

- Immigration status. Refers to a person's authorization to enter, remain, and work in a country as a foreign national. It is determined by the immigration laws and regulations of the country in question. Immigration status can include categories such as permanent resident, temporary worker, student, refugee, or undocumented immigrant. In many cases, a person's immigration status can affect their legal status. For example, a person who is not authorized to work in a country may not have the legal status to enter into contracts or own property. Similarly, an undocumented immigrant may not have the legal status to access certain legal remedies. It includes the process for residency, the refugee or asylum seekers status determination, etc.

- Registration documents.  Information related to the documentation and data required by governments and other authorities to regulate the movement of individuals across borders. This can include information such as visa, stamp or entry record in the passport, proof of legal entry, and other forms of identification.

- Diplomas, validation of certificates, and school records. Information related to the student’s academic records and the recognition of diplomas/certificates of individuals who have studied or worked in another country and wish to continue their education or career in a new location. 

- Other legal documents. Information related to other legal documents, such as contracts and agreements, bills of sale, etc.

Without proper identification documents, individuals may find it difficult or impossible to travel, and to access a range of basic services (e.g., education, healthcare, adequate housing, financial services, etc.), and have a political, social, and economic life (e.g., vote, access to employment opportunities, implementation of legal business activity, etc.).

nodes.name: Freedom of movement
nodes.definition:
Information related to all restrictions and barriers to freedom of movement, including forced displacement, siege, movement restrictions imposed by government/authority, mine/UXOs/IED inhibiting the movement of populations, or any other situation when a person does not have free choice related to movements. Freedom of movement includes a range of rights and protections, such as the right to move freely within one's own country without restrictions; the right to leave any country at will; the right to leave one's own country and return to it at will; the right to seek asylum or protection in another country if one's own country is unable or unwilling to provide protection from persecution or harm; the right to be protected from refoulement or forced return to a place/country where one may face persecution or harm; the right to be protected from arbitrary or unlawful detention, including restrictions on movement; the right (and ability) to move and choose one’s residence freely and in safety within the territory of the State (including in and out of camps and settlements), without undue influence or interference, regardless of the length of stay or the reason or purpose of the move. 

- Forced displacement. Information related to individuals and communities having been forced or obliged to flee or to leave their homes or places of habitual residence. It can be as a result of or in order to avoid the effects of shock/events or situations such as generalized violence, human rights abuses, and/or development projects (e.g., dams, mines, urbanization, etc.). The defining factor is the absence of will or consent. In both cases, it includes situations where people have fled or situations where people have been forcibly removed from their homes, evicted or relocated to another place not of their choosing, whether by State or non-State actors, such as: expulsion/removal from territory, deportation, collective/mass expulsions, etc.
 
- Siege. Information related to the military encirclement of an area with the imposition of restrictions on the entry and exit of people and essential goods, with the aim of forcing its surrender.

- Forced return of IDPs. Information related to the attempted or successful coercion of IDPs to return to their areas of habitual residence, which places their lives, safety, liberty and/or health at risk. Coercion need not necessarily require the open use of force. IDPs can be coerced into return through any actions by responsible parties intended to result in return (e.g., stopping the provision of essential utilities to camps or closing existing shelters).

- Refoulement of refugees or asylum-seekers. Information related to the attempted or successful coercion of refugees or asylum-seekers to return to their countries/territories/areas of habitual residence, which places their lives, safety, liberty and/or health at risk. Coercion need not necessarily require the open use of force. Refugees or asylum-seekers can be coerced into return through any actions by responsible parties intended to result in return (for example halted provisions of essential utilities to camps or closure of existing shelters).

- Denial of entry and denial of access to asylum process after entry. Information related to the denial, by a State, of protection/asylum on its territory to persons outside their country of nationality or habitual residence who are fleeing persecution or serious harm. It includes the reception issues (e.g., attitude of the border/immigration public officials).

- Movement restriction. Information related to situations which require the government/authority to temporarily restrict freedom of movement, such as: 
a) Official rules implemented to limit people’s ability to enter or depart the country or travel freely within a country. It includes intensified border controls, partial border closures, international flights suspension, visa restrictions or suspensions, restrictions or suspensions of domestic travel, closure of public transport, requirements of health documents at border points, requirement of sanitary documents/pass in order to access to public or private buildings, etc.
b) Emergency protocol imposed by governmental authorities requiring people to stay in their homes, or preventing/limiting their activities outside of their home, in order to reduce specific risks to themselves or to others. It includes quarantine, curfews, lockdown, etc.

The restrictions to freedom of movement prescribed by law should be necessary and proportionate to achieve a legitimate aim (such as protect national security or public order, health or morals, or the rights or freedoms of others), and be non-discriminatory and consistent with other human, civil and political rights.

Typical examples:
Movement restrictions can take many forms, including unlawful restrictions; unlawful refoulement/interception at border; lack of adequate infrastructure, damaged roads and bridges, lack of safe and affordable transport; poor physical condition owing to age, ill-health or disability that limit people’s ability to travel; 
General travel restrictions, either legal or administrative, which regulate movement within the country (e.g., from rural to urban areas). These can include curfews, restricted traveling hours or days, restrictions on travel distances, or strict travel criteria, such as need for specific documentation or travel permits; 
Targeted travel restrictions (e.g. on movement in and out of camps or settlements for displaced persons). These can include curfews, restrictive traveling hours or days, restrictions on travel distances, strict exit/entry criteria, and documentation requirements; 
Physical barriers such as walls or checkpoints; 
Legal or administrative restrictions such as travel bans or visa requirements.

nodes.name: Housing, Land and Property (HLP)
nodes.definition:
Information related to the right to adequate housing and safe living environment that support the dignity and the recovery of people affected by crisis and enable essential household and livelihood activities in and around the home. This includes the full spectrum of violations of rights to HLP held according to statutory customary or unformal law, both public and private, such as: 

- The tenure rights. Information related to the legal right that an individual or entity holds in ownership/leasehold of housing, land, and property. Tenure rights determine the rights, privileges, and limitations associated with housing, land, and property, such as the right to occupy, use, transfer, or encumber the property. Tenure rights can be held by various parties, including owners, tenants, cooperative dwellers, customary land tenure owners and users, informal sector dwellers without secure tenure, etc. It includes issues related to the lack of legal recognition of tenure rights, lack of formal documentation (e.g., rental contract, property title, etc.), disputes between owners and renters, absence of formal agreement with owners, occupation of properties, etc. Land rights are rights held to both land and natural assets. It includes issues related to land documentation, disputes over ownership of land/natural resources, disputes over right of use of land/natural resources, land concentration, land speculation, encroachment, land grabbing, etc. 

- The insecurity of tenure. Information related to the protection of an occupant's right to remain in a property. Security of tenure is the foundation of the right to adequate housing and many other human rights. It guarantees legal protection to tenants or occupants against forced eviction from the property without proper notice or legal grounds. This includes insecurity of tenure, eviction from HLP, forced eviction from house/occupied site/camp, house demolition, fear of eviction, etc. 
Various elements, separately or combined, define a forced eviction:
- The permanent or temporary removal of individuals, families and/or communities from the homes and/or land which they occupy;
- The removal is carried out against the will of the occupants, with or without the use of force;
- The removal is carried out without the provision of proper alternative housing and relocation, adequate compensation and/or access to productive land, when appropriate;
- The removal is carried out without the possibility of challenging either the decision or the process of eviction, without due process and disregarding the State’s national and international obligations.
It can be related to urban and rural development, transformation and/or zoning, mining, extractive and other industrial activities, land acquisitions and leases, privatization and/or speculation, lack of legal security of tenure, legislation or changes related to housing and land, discriminatory laws and practices, non-deliverance or non-recognition of titles, slum clearance, land grabbing (including by armed groups and paramilitaries), unaffordability, defaulting on payments, housing tenure linked to employment permits, etc. Type of security/insecurity of tenure include:
HHs who own their own dwelling with property rights, 
HHs who own their own dwelling with no property title but can obtain them,
HHs who own their own dwelling with no property title and cannot obtain, prove ownership,
HHs who rent their dwelling and have a written rental contract, can renew contract or obtain a new one,
HHs who rent their dwelling and have a written rental contract, cannot renew contract or obtain a new one,
HHs who rent their dwelling and do not have a written rental contract,
HHs who were granted their dwelling by organizations/authorities with permission, and able/not able to stay as much as needed,
HHs who were granted their dwelling by relatives/family/community/others with permission,
HHs who squat without permission, and able/not able to stay as much as needed,
 HHs with risk of eviction after/within the next XX months,
HHs who cannot reinstall into the same property in their place of origin (HLP destroyed, land robbed, house occupied, house too small, etc.).

- The systems and regulations. Information related to the existence and fulfillment of the legal, administrative, and institutional frameworks that govern housing, land, and property ownership, use, and management. It encompasses a range of laws, policies, procedures, and practices, such as: laws related to land use planning, urban planning, zoning regulations, building codes, mechanisms for resolving land disputes, property boundary disputes, or tenancy disputes, and environmental protection laws related to shelter and settlement. 

- The inadequacy of housing. Information related to:
Shelter unaffordable, i.e., that does not allow individual/HHs to attain other essential goods and services, and to live in dignity once they have paid the rent,
Shelter inhabitable, i.e., an environment that does not enables healthy and dignified domestic living, and does not provide physical safety and security, such as: dwelling unit that does not meet physical quality standards of housing (structural safety, weatherproofing, and permeance to water/air/cold), unsafe and unprotected interior domestic living space, substandard housing, 
Slums and informal settlements,
Settlement overcrowded, or lack of usable space for public/outdoor activities,
Shelter culturally unacceptable,
Shelter inaccessible and inoperable for persons facing mobility barriers,
Livelihood opportunities and essential community services out of access range from shelter/settlement,
Shelters that are difficult to access or located in hazardous/insecure areas.

- The destruction of personal property. Information related to partial or total damage and destruction of property caused by unlawful acts, committed wilfully or wantonly (done recklessly and with a conscious disregard for substantial harm to people or property). Unless such destruction is imperatively required by the necessities of a conflict.

- The confiscation of personal property. Information related to the seizure of the property of an enemy, unless such seizure is imperatively required by the necessities of the conflict.

- The continued occupation of personal property/expropriation. Information related to any expropriation or prolonged occupation of private property, directly or indirectly, by Government or by armed forces.

nodes.name: Human, civil and political rights
nodes.definition:
Information related to the respect or the violation of the rights that guarantee equal social opportunities and equal protection under the laws regardless of race, gender, ethnicity, religion or other personal characteristics and status including being displaced or belonging to a minority group. Human, civil and political rights are a class of rights that protect individuals' freedom and liberties from infringement by governments, social organizations, and private individuals. It includes a wide range of individual liberties, rights and protection mechanisms such as:

- Right to life. Information related to the respect or violation of the right that protects against arbitrary/unlawful killings, death caused by attacks against civilians, death penalty, extrajudicial/summary execution, and man slaughtering. This right asserts that every individual has the inherent right to life, and that no one shall be arbitrarily deprived of their life.

- Right to liberty. Information related to the respect or violation of the right that protects against arbitrary arrest, detention, imprisonment, or exile and guarantees not to be detained or imprisoned except in accordance with the law, and with due process and fair trial rights. It encompasses any form of deprivation of liberty as a result of arrest or detention, such as by the police or other agents of the State, or confinement to a certain location, institution or facility. The right to liberty prohibits any form of deprivation of liberty that is either unlawful (i.e. not provided for by law or carried out in accordance with the law) and/or arbitrary (e.g. is unjust, unreasonable or disproportionate), such as: 
Abduction, kidnapping or enforced/involuntary disappearance, forced recruitment into armed forces/group or compulsory drafting, slavery, trafficking in persons, deprivation of liberty without just cause,
Not be informed promptly of the reasons for the arrest or detention, in a language one understands,
Not be brought promptly before a judge to confirm the lawfulness of arrest/detention,
Not be provided with access to legal counsel and to the courts to challenge the lawfulness of the detention. 

- Right to physical integrity. Information related to the respect or violation of the right to freedom from torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment (such as threat, intimidation, harassment, humiliation, theft, robbery, extortion, physical assault or abuses, and excessive use of force).

- Right to privacy. Information related to the respect or the arbitrary/unlawful interference with one's home, family, or private life, as well as the right to the protection of one's personal data and identity. It includes:
Any intrusion into a person's private life, family, home, or correspondence that is not authorized by law or is not necessary to achieve a legitimate purpose, e.g., surveillance, searches, or seizures of property or information without a valid warrant or other legal basis.
Any unauthorized access, use, disclosure, or alteration of personal information, such as names, addresses, financial information, or other identifying data, that can be used to identify an individual. Such breaches can result in identity theft, financial fraud, or other harms to an individual's reputation, privacy, and security.

- Right to freedom of thought, conscience, and religion. Information related to the respect or violation of freedom of thought, belief, as well as the right to practice one's religion or belief without interference from the State or other individuals. It includes:
The freedom to choose and practice one's own religion or belief system, or to choose not to follow any religion or belief system,
The freedom to manifest one's religion or belief in worship, observance, practice, and teaching,
The right to worship alone or with others, and to establish religious institutions and communities, and to observe religious holidays and ceremonies,
The right to change religions or belief systems, or to hold and express one's own beliefs without fear of persecution or punishment,
Not be forced to adopt a particular religion or belief system against one's will,
Not being discriminated against on the basis of religion or belief system.

- Right to freedom of opinion/information/expression. Information related to the respect or violation of the ability to form and hold opinions or thoughts without interference, and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds without interference from the State or other individuals. It includes the right to seek/receive/impart information through any forms of communication, the right to access to information of public interest from a variety of sources, the right of the media to receive information, the right of the public to receive media output, the right of individuals to seek and receive information from public bodies, and the right to hold those in power accountable without fear of retaliation or persecution. It may be subject to restrictions, prescribed by law, aimed at protecting the rights of others or public interests.

- Right to freedom of peaceful assembly and association. Information related to the respect or violation of the right to peaceful assembly and association with others, as well as the right to form and join groups and other associations. An assembly is an intentional and temporary gathering which may take place in a private or public place and can be planned or spontaneous. This right is essential for the protection of other human rights, such as the right to freedom of expression and the right to participate in public life. It may be subject to restrictions, prescribed by law, aimed at protecting the rights of others or public interests. It includes:
The freedom to gather with others in a peaceful manner, whether for political, social, cultural, or religious purposes. This includes the right to organize, hold, and participate to public meetings, marches, demonstrations, and peaceful protests,
The freedom to form and join associations or groups, including political parties, trade unions, and other organizations,
The freedom to form and join groups to advocate for their interests, and to hold those in power accountable.

- Right to participate in public affairs and elections. Information related to the right to participate in the political life/process/governance of one's country and in public discourse on issues that affect one's life, without discrimination based on race, gender, religion, or other factors. It includes:
The right to vote, i.e., the right to participate in the election of the government representatives,
The right to stand for election, i.e., to become a candidate for political office and to represent one's views and interests in the political process,
The right to engage in political activities, including the right to join and form political parties,
The right to express opinions on political issues and to have one's voice heard in decision-making processes.

- Equality before the law. Information related to equal access to justice and legal protection, and be subject to the same laws and legal procedures for everyone, regardless of their status or position. The principle of equality before the law is essential for ensuring that justice is administered fairly and impartially, and that individuals are not subjected to discrimination or bias in the legal process. It includes:
The right to a fair trial (as the accused). The right to a fair trial means that every person has the right to have their case heard in a competent, independent, and impartial court or tribunal, with full respect for their legal rights and the presumption of innocence. It includes the right to legal counsel/legal representation/interpreter, the right to be informed of the charges against one’s, the right to a public trial, the right to be judged without undue delays, and the right to challenge the evidence presented against one’s.
The presumption of innocence. The presumption of innocence is a key element of the right to a fair trial, which asserts that every person is considered innocent until proven guilty in a fair and impartial trial. This means that the burden of proof rests with the prosecution to demonstrate the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the accused is not required to prove their innocence.

- Right to family life. Information related with the ability to marry/start/found a family and any restrictions on marriage, based on ethnicity, national origin, religion or caste. A family is defined as all those who consider themselves and are considered by each other, to be part of a family, and who wish to live together. Permissible restrictions on the right to marry include restrictions with regard to marriage among relatives as well as the introduction of a minimum age of marriage.

- Right to nationality. Information related with the right of each individual to acquire/change/retain a nationality, and arbitrary denial or deprivation of nationality/ citizenship, either because of a national law or because of particular circumstances. Denial of nationality can lead to statelessness status. Deprivation of nationality takes place when a person loses or is stripped of his or her nationality or citizenship as a result of discriminatory national legislations.

nodes.name: Justice and rule of law
nodes.definition:
Information related to the fair and impartial treatment of individuals, based on the principles of equality, fairness, and ethics. The concept of Justice involves the idea that individuals should be treated equally and fairly, without discrimination or prejudice, and that they should be held accountable for their actions, but also that they should be given the opportunity to defend themselves and have their voices heard. Within a State, Justice is the set of institutions that impose the rule of law. The rule of law is a principle that establishes the supremacy of the law over individuals and institutions. It means that everyone, regardless of their position or power, must abide by the same set of laws and regulations. The rule of law ensures that the law is fair, predictable, and transparent, and that no one is above it.In a society that upholds the rule of law, the legal system is independent of political and personal influences. The law is enforced equally, without discrimination or favoritism, and individuals have the right to a fair trial and due process. The rule of law also implies that laws must be clear and understandable, and that individuals have the right to challenge laws that they believe are unjust or unconstitutional. Fair and just enforcement of laws means that the laws are applied equally to everyone, without discrimination or bias. It means that individuals who break the law are held accountable, but they are also treated with respect and dignity, and their rights are protected.
Fair and just enforcement of laws requires that law enforcement officers and other government officials act with integrity and impartiality. They must follow established procedures and protocols, and their decisions should be based on evidence and the law, rather than personal opinions or biases. Fair and just enforcement of laws requires that the justice system is accessible to everyone, regardless of their socioeconomic status or background. It means that individuals have access to legal representation, and that they are not disadvantaged by their race, ethnicity, gender, or any other characteristic. Access to justice should include the access to legal notices and information, the availability and affordability of legal assistance, the presence of substantive and procedural safeguards recognized in international law, the access to counseling and legal support. The justice system encompasses: 

a) The legal system, sometimes also called ‘‘judicial power’’. It is the set of laws, courts and magistrates who judge offenses. The justice system is responsible for:
- Enforcing the laws of the authority in place, legitimate or not, through interpretation of laws, investigation and prosecution, adjudication, sentencing, and appeals.
- Ensuring that everyone is treated fairly under the law. It means that everyone, regardless of their status or position, should have equal access to justice and legal protections, and be subject to the same laws and legal procedures. The principle of equality before the law is essential for ensuring that justice is administered fairly and impartially, and that individuals are not subjected to discrimination or bias in the legal process. It includes:
- The right to a fair trial (as the accused). The right to a fair trial means that every person has the right to have their case heard in a competent, independent, and impartial court or tribunal, with full respect for their legal rights and the presumption of innocence. It includes be provided with access to legal counsel/legal representation/interpreter and the courts to challenge the lawfulness of the detention, be brought promptly before a judge to confirm the lawfulness of arrest/detention, be informed promptly of the reasons (charges) for the arrest or detention, in a language one understands.
- The presumption of innocence. The presumption of innocence is a key element of the right to a fair trial, which asserts that every person is considered innocent until proven guilty in a fair and impartial trial. This means that the burden of proof rests with the prosecution to demonstrate the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, and that the accused is not required to prove their innocence.

The denial of access to justice relates to the impediments to access to judicial mechanisms, processes, and remedies, ranging from access to statutory courts or commissions to traditional mechanisms such as customary or faith-based dispute resolution bodies. It can manifest even when legal and policy procedures are in place, if the mechanisms are not accessible, affordable, adequate, and timely. 

The denial of access to remedies (for the victims) includes all impediments to obtain effective procedural and substantive remedies following legal claims. Procedural remedies include regulations, laws, processes, and entitlements. Substantive remedies include effective remedies at the conclusion of the processes – such as obtaining redress, restitution, fair and adequate compensation, rehabilitation, or others. 

The lack of due process can manifest through:
The denial of notification: the accused does not receive proper notice of the charges or allegations against one, which prevents him from properly preparing one’s defense.
The lack of a fair hearing: the accused is denied the opportunity to present evidence, cross-examine witnesses and have a neutral decision-maker. These safeguards are essential for a fair hearing, and their absence can result in biased or arbitrary decisions.
The inadequate legal representation: the accused does not have access to a lawyer/legal counsel or does not receive sufficient assistance, making it challenging for one to navigate the legal process effectively.
The lack of impartiality: judicial or administrative decision-makers must be unbiased and neutral. Lack of impartiality can lead to decisions influenced by personal biases or conflicts of interest.
The denial of  appeal or review: the accused has no opportunity to appeal or seek review of a decision, which deprives one of the chance to challenge errors or injustices committed during the process.
The failure to provide evidence: withholding evidence or failing to disclose it to the accused undermines one’s ability to mount a proper defense.
Voir dans cette liste ce qui s'applique + trier ce qui est déjà pris en compte : any violation of the rule of law, equality before the law, due process, presumption of innocence, stare decisis, equity, natural justice, separation of powers, constitutional supremacy, judicial independence, protection of fundamental rights and freedoms, legality principle (in criminal law), good faith (bonne foi), legal certainty (sécurité juridique), proportionality, non-retroactivity of laws, res Judicata, primacy of written norms.


b) The law enforcement agencies, meaning the government organizations responsible for enforcing the law, maintaining public order, and protecting the safety and security of citizens. These agencies are responsible for investigating crimes, apprehending suspects, and bringing them to justice. It includes police departments, gendarmerie, sheriff's offices, State police agencies, etc. Law enforcement officers (police officers, cops, etc.) are authorized to use force when necessary to protect themselves and others, but they are also required to act within the limits of the law and respect the rights of individuals. 

Abuse of force by law enforcement agencies or officers refers to situations where excessive force is used in a way that violates an individual's rights or causes unnecessary harm, such as:
Using deadly force when it is not necessary, 
Using excessive force during arrests or interrogations such as chokeholds or neck restraints, 
Making unlawful arrest. Arrest is the taking of a person into legal custody, as by officers of the law. Arrest can be unlawful if for example it has been done without informing immediately of the reason for arrest, in a language one understands and/or not being brought promptly before a judge to confirm the lawfulness of arrest/detention.
Engaging in racial profiling or discriminatory practices. 

Victims from abuse of force should have legal remedies available to them, such as the ability to report, file a complaint, sue for damages and seek redress for such actions. It is also important that officers can be held accountable for their actions.

nodes.name: Mine, UXOs and IEDs
nodes.definition:
Information related to the harm (death or injury) or exposure to harm caused by Explosive Ordnance (EO) hazards and hazardous areas. This includes mines, cluster munitions, unexploded ordnance, abandoned ordnance, booby traps, improvised explosive devices and other devices (as defined by the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons: Amended Protocol II). It includes events, accidents, as well as the presence of suspected or confirmed hazardous areas. Mines and other explosive ordnance can:
- Incapacitate, injure, or kill one or more persons. Victims include directly impacted individuals (casualties), families and affected communities in the short and long-term term, and their primary and secondary, intended, or unintended effects such as the emotional/psychological, and physical consequences of injuries caused by explosive ordnance. The term ‘survivor’ refers to a person who was injured because of explosive ordnance and has survived the accident.
- Prevent people from accessing resources, livelihoods, and opportunities due to the fear of the presence of explosive ordnance. The social and economic consequences of the presence of mines and explosive ordnance can be the inaccessibility or inability to use essential infrastructure such as roads and markets (this can limit access to schools, hospitals, shelter, food, etc.), or the inability or reduced ability to pursue livelihood activities such as use of agricultural land or water sources. This can limit access to food/water, and generate lack of income and economic losses.

Signatory’s States of the Antipersonnel Mine Ban Treaty are obliged to provide assistance for the care and rehabilitation, and social and economic reintegration, of mine victims and for mine awareness programmes. Victim assistance is a set of concrete actions to meet the immediate and long-term needs of mine/ERW victims, their families, affected communities and persons with disabilities.

nodes.name: Physical safety and security
nodes.definition:
Information related to the exposure of individual to violence, threats, harassment such as: abduction/kidnapping (enforced disappearance, unlawful arrest, arbitrary arrest or arbitrary detention), attacks against civilians, attacks against civilians objects, forced family separation, discrimination, stigmatization, hate speech, denial of resources, opportunities and services, forced recruitment/compulsory drafting of a person over the age of 18, psychological/emotional abuse or inflected distress, theft, robbery, extorsion, killing, torture or cruel, inhuman, degrading treatment or punishment, trafficking in persons, forced labour, and slavery-like practices.

- Abduction and kidnapping. Information related to removal, seizure, capture, apprehension, taking or enforced disappearance of a person either temporarily or permanently, with support or acquiescence of the State. 
a) Enforced disappearance is constituted by three cumulative elements: 1) the person is detained or otherwise deprived of liberty, 2) the deprivation of liberty is carried out by State agents, or by persons or groups of persons acting with the State’s support or acquiescence, and, 3) those responsible refuse to acknowledge the detention, or conceal the concerned person’s fate or whereabouts, placing the person outside the protection of the law.
b) Unlawful arrest describes the initial act of taking a person into detention that is not based on either a criminal charge or another reason provided for by law (established in national law and carried out in accordance with procedures). A detention is considered unlawful when it is not in accordance with national laws and the procedures established by law (e.g., without proper legal justification, without charges, without informing immediately of the reason for arrest, in a language one understands, without being brought promptly before a judge to confirm the lawfulness of arrest/detention, and when there is unlawful pre-trial detention, or detention beyond a reasonable timeframe). 
c) Arbitrary arrest or arbitrary detention refers to the situation where the arrest or detention is not justified by a legitimate purpose, reasonable, appropriate and necessary in the individual’s particular circumstance. A detention is arbitrary when it is inappropriate, unjust, unreasonable, or unnecessary in the circumstances. It includes: detention based on counter-terrorism laws which provides for long administrative detention to bypass normal criminal justice processes; detention as a punishment for political opponent/human rights defenders or based on discriminatory grounds; arrests linked to a possible criminal charge where there is no reasonable suspicion that a person has committed the offense; person due to appear before a court arrested even though the person’s presence could have been secured by other means; arrest on a criminal charge without arrest warrant (except if a person is about to commit a crime or is caught in the act).
 
- Attacks against civilians and civilian objects in a context of armed conflict. Information related to any deliberate or non-deliberate attack by parties to a conflict against the civilian population and civilian objects, whether in offense or in defense, even if the attack does not lead to the death or injury of civilians. It encompasses civilians injured, civilians killed, and attacks with direct impact on civilians or civilian infrastructures.
Civilian population comprises all persons who do not belong to any of the various categories of combatants defined in the Geneva Convention and its Additional Protocols, i.e., persons who are not members of the armed forces and do not take part in hostilities.
Civilian objects are defined as all objects that are not military objectives. Towns, cities, villages, residential areas, dwellings, buildings, houses, schools, civilian means of transportation, hospitals, places of worship, displacement sites and cultural property are normally used for civilian purposes, and, as such, should not be subjects of attack, especially the objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population.
Attacks can be perpetrated by State or non-State actors, intentionally or unintentionally, and causing harm to civilian population and objects directly or indirectly. Unlawful attacks can result from:
A direct attack against civilians,
An indiscriminate attack: 1) when they do not distinguish between military and civilian population or objects (e.g. bombing a highly populated area); 2) whether the use of methods or means of warfare cannot be directed at a specific military objective; 3) the effects of which cannot be limited, (e.g. the use of cluster munitions in densely populated urban areas, the use of biological weapons and the use of mines in populated urban areas).
A disproportionate attack: when a party to the conflict carries out an attack on a military target which can be expected to cause loss of civilian life or injury to civilians or damage to civilian objects, which would be excessive (disproportionate) in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated (principle of proportionality).
 
- Forced family separation. Information related to all situations when family members are separated, including children from their parents or caregivers, persons with disabilities or older persons, due to violent conflicts, climate induced disasters and other crises. Forced separation disrupts the relative’s relationship and might expose them to various dangers and heightened risks of exploitation, neglect and abuse.
  
- Discrimination, stigmatization, denial of resources, opportunities, and services. Information related with acts that deprive or pre-empt people to rightfully access economic resources/assets or livelihood opportunities, education, health or other social services, on the basis of unjustifiable and/or unlawful reasons or policies with the consent or under the acquiescence or negligence of public officials or responsible parties. Discrimination includes acts of making unjustified distinctions between human beings based on categories to which they are perceived to belong (race, age, religion, as well as other categories). It encompasses any situation where people are excluded from the use or enjoyment of resources, facilities, assets, or rights. This includes all situations where people encounter barriers to access and have no alternatives, or where people are threatened with violence and fear for their physical and psychological/emotional integrity, e.g., barriers to HLP (distorted access to land and employment), barriers to education (a girl prevented from attending school), barriers to livelihoods, access to services; discriminatory social norms and practice, discriminatory laws or customary practices denying access or decision-making to land, household property, decent work or financial resources (earnings forcibly taken by an intimate partner or family member,  widow prevented from receiving an inheritance). 
Stigma can include dehumanizing, degrading, discrediting and devaluing people in certain population groups, often based on a feeling of disgust. Stigma and discrimination are closely interrelated, and they reinforce each other. Stigma often lies at the root of discrimination and provides a justification to discrimination as ‘natural’ and necessary and makes systemic discrimination possible. One person can possess different attributes to which stigma is attached.
Denial of equal opportunity, including resources and services refers to any action, conduct or measure resulting in or likely to result in the taking away in any manner of existing opportunities for livelihood, vocation, occupation or employment or any other livelihood rights and entitlements.
 
- Forced recruitment of a person over the age of 18. Information related to all situations in which a person over the age of 18 is compelled to join armed forces or group, by means of coercion, threats of any harm or other means.
 
- Psychological/emotional abuse or inflected distress. Information related to direct acts perpetrated with the intention of causing psychological/emotional pains or injuries, as well as the indirect results of such acts, and the psychological/emotional health consequences of conflict and emergencies. It includes all emotional/psychological (such as emotions, thoughts, behaviors) and psychosocial (such as interpersonal relationships and social connections, social resources, social norms, social values, social roles, community life, spiritual and religious life) harm, and the presence of conditions that generate prolonged mental health and emotional/psychological well-being problems not addressed by State authorities, including not ensuring the availability of and accessibility to support systems. Examples include:
New or exacerbation of pre-existing mental health and psychological/emotional well-being problems,
Traumatic experiences, often resulting from loss of family members, participation in or witnessing of violent acts, breakdown of social services such as health and education, threats of physical violence, intimidation, humiliation, forced isolation, stalking, verbal harassment, unwanted attention, remarks, gestures or written words of menacing nature, destruction of cherished things,
Post-traumatic stress,
Depression/anxiety or mental disorder due to direct exposure to traumatic events and exposure to increased levels of daily stressors.
 
- Theft/robbery, extortion. Information related with unlawful dispossession of persons, either individually or collectively, involving a direct or indirect responsibility of public officials or non-State actors, either by acts or by omissions. Theft/robbery includes looting, pillage, and any other act of stealing. Extortion includes any practice or form of coercion, such as the unjustified use of force, violence or intimidation, actual or threatened, to obtain actions, money or property from a person or entity. For example: levying illegal taxes, levying ‘‘taxes’’ in return for safety, abuse of authority such as bribery/corruption.

- Torture or cruel, inhuman, degrading treatment or punishment. Information related to any intentional acts that causes or results in severe pain or suffering, whether physical or psychological/emotional, for purposes such as: obtaining personal information or a confession, punishing an act the person has committed or is suspected of having committed, intimidating or coercing him/her, any reason based on discrimination of any kind by a public official, either directly or indirectly, or non-State actors (e.g. personnel in detention facilities or de facto authorities). It also includes any other act of cruel, inhuman, degrading/humiliating treatment or punishment, and outrages upon personal dignity. These acts may be targeting a person in relation to a third person and may include: beatings or blunt trauma, shaking, suspension in painful positions, stabbing, puncture wounds, amputation, removal of nails, burns, hot fluids, acid, forced ingestion, injections, electric shocks, asphyxiation, death threats, mock executions, witness torture of another person, sleep deprivation, overcrowding, solitary confinement, withholding of food or water, sensory deprivation, exposure to extreme light or sound, use of animals, positional torture, rape, forced nudity, denial of access to food/medical-treatment/recreation/contact with the outside world for persons deprived of liberty, mutilation and maiming. Although physical assault or abuse can constitute torture, it is not always torture. Unlike in torture, the perpetrator needs not to have any particular purpose in inflicting the suffering. Torture requires the existence of a specific purpose behind the act – to obtain information, for example. Torture or cruel, inhuman, degrading treatment or punishment are generally more prevalent when:
Criminal law does not include torture as an offense,
No prohibition against torture is included in trainings of law enforcement personnel, civil or military, medical personnel, public officials and other persons involved in custody, interrogation or treatment of individuals,
No complaints on allegations of torture acts are being allowed.
 
- Trafficking in persons, forced labor and slavery-like practices. Information related to the harm (recruitment, transportation, transfer, harboring or receipt of persons), the means (threat or use of force, coercion, abduction, fraud, deception, abuse of power, abuse of position of vulnerability, giving or receiving payments or benefits) used to achieve the consent of a person having control over another person, and the purpose of the exploitation (forced labor or services, slavery or practices similar to slavery, servitude, organ removal). If one of those means has been used, the consent of a victim of human trafficking to exploitation is considered as irrelevant.
Forced labor refers to situations in which persons are coerced to work under the menace of any penalty, for example through the use of violence or intimidation, or by more subtle means such as accumulated debt, retention of identity papers or threats of denunciation to immigration authorities. Forced labor includes debt bondage and slavery. Slavery is the status or condition of a person or persons over whom any or all of the powers of ownership are exercised. Slavery includes the purchasing, selling, lending or bartering of a person or persons, and other similar deprivation of liberty. 
 
- Harassment. Information related to all acts of systematic and annoying actions of one party or a group, including threats and demands. The purposes include racial prejudice, personal malice, attempting to force someone to quit a job, applying illegal pressure to collect a bill, verbal harassment, or merely gain sadistic pleasure from making someone fearful or anxious.

- Hate speech. Information related to any form of communication, expression, or language that promotes or incites violence, discrimination, hostility, or prejudice against individuals or groups based on attributes such as their race, ethnicity, religion, nationality or other characteristics.
 
- Physical assault or abuse (not related to Sexual Gender Based Violence). Information related to acts of physical violence that are not sexual in nature. Examples include: hitting, slapping, choking, cutting, shoving, burning, or any other act that results in pain, discomfort or injury.

- Medical or scientific experiments.  Information related to medical and scientific experiment or any other medical procedure not indicated by the state of health of the person concerned, not consistent with generally accepted medical standards, or without free and informed consent.

- Killing. Information related to deprivation of life, either as a result of the use of force or due to any other action or omission.

nodes.name: Sexual and Gender-Based Violence (SGBV)
nodes.definition:
Information related to any harmful (or threat of harmful) act perpetrated against a person’s will and based on socially ascribed (i.e., gender) differences between males and females. It includes any act (or threats of acts) that results in, or is likely to result in, physical, sexual or emotional/psychological harm or suffering, coercion and other deprivations of liberty. It can happen both in public and private spaces. Women and girls experience multiple forms of SGBV due to systemic gender inequality and other forms of intersectional discrimination including ableism, racism, nationalism and other structures of power. It includes:

- Sexual violence. Information related to the exposure of an individual to any form of non-consensual sexual contact, activity or behavior that involves the use of force, coercion, or manipulation against a person's will.  It includes sexual violence, or sexual threats/harassment such as: rape (the non-consensual penetration, however slight, of the vagina, anus or mouth with a penis or other body part or any object), attempted rape,  sexual assault, unwanted kissing, fondling, or touching of genitalia and buttocks, force nudity, gestures/stalking/verbal harassment/remarks/written words of a sexual nature. 
- Intimate partner violence,
- Other forms of domestic violence,
- Forced domestic labor,
- Forced and/or coerced prostitution,
- Trafficking for sexual exploitation,
- Child marriage,
- Forced marriage (marriage of an individual against their will),
- Female infanticide,
- Forced pregnancy,
- Hate speech based on gender or sexual orientation,
- Discrimination, stigmatization, denial of resources, opportunities, and services based on gender or sexual orientation,
- So called “honor” crimes,
- Harmful Traditional Practices (e.g., Female Genital Mutilation/cutting).

Certain forms of sexual violence can also be directed against men and boys, particularly in armed conflict and detention, aimed at emasculating the individual, and/or reinforcing traditional, cultural, or normative conceptions on masculinity or femininity. 
Gender discrimination is also the cause of many forms of violence against people of other sexual orientation and gender identity.
