nodes.question: Where are people subjected to forced domestic labor, coerced prostitution, or trafficking for sexual purposes, and who is most exposed?

nodes.name: Sexual Violence Patterns and Settings
nodes.definition: Information related to non-consensual sexual contact or coercion—including rape, attempted rape, sexual assault, unwanted touching, forced nudity, stalking, and sexual harassment or threats—affecting women, girls, men, boys, and persons of diverse SOGIESC in public or private settings, including conflict and detention.
nodes.question: What forms, locations, and patterns of sexual violence—including against men, boys, and diverse SOGIESC persons—are reported, and which groups are most at risk?

nodes.name: Survivor Support Law and Public Awareness
nodes.l3: Survivor Support Law and Public Awareness
nodes.definition: Information related to availability and quality of medical, psychosocial, safety, and justice support for SGBV survivors; gaps in legal frameworks or enforcement that leave victims unprotected; and community education activities that shape reporting and help-seeking.
nodes.question: What medical, psychosocial, safety, and justice support exists for SGBV survivors, and where do service, legal, or public-awareness gaps leave people unprotected?

nodes.name: Shelter
nodes.definition: Information related to people’s living conditions and housing arrangements, including the adequacy, safety and dignity of where and how households live. It covers domestic living space and privacy; dwelling type, materials and structural condition; housing, land and property tenure arrangements; non-food household items needed for daily life and shelter maintenance; and settlement scenarios for displaced and non-displaced populations. It is used to classify content on shelter adequacy, security of tenure and the household environment.
nodes.question: How adequate, safe and secure are people’s dwellings, living spaces, household items, tenure arrangements and settlement conditions, and where do structural, HLP or settlement gaps most undermine dignity and recovery?

nodes.name: Domestic living space
nodes.definition:
Information related to the living space, including privacy/space, safety, household items, being functional, and allowing dignity.

Privacy/space. The living space to perform basic domestic activities, such as:
Family life (e.g., number of people living in the shelter, number of people per room, number of separated rooms per household, interior partitions, or internal subdivisions, etc.),
Food preparation. Place for cooking (in a separate room, in a separate building, in veranda, in porch, in open air, in communal space, further away, etc.),
Sleeping. Enough place for sleeping/sex, enough sleeping place/household size,

Safe and protected interior for domestic life, such as:
Ventilation. Properly management or evacuation of the condensation, humidity, smoke from cooking/heating/lighting, 
Electricity (e.g., access to electricity, number of hours of electricity/day, electricity available in or out of the premises, etc.),
Fire safety (e.g., non-inflammable base for heating stove, safe distance for storage of fuel, etc.), 
Heating/cooling (access to heating/cooling when needed), 
Safe and affordable energy to maintain thermal comfort (heating/cooling) and provide lighting, 
Internal floor-to-ceiling height, 
Disease vector protection, long-lasting insecticide-treated nets,
Culturally appropriate interior for domestic family life.

Safety/security related to the outside world 
Possibility of locking/protecting the shelter against intrusion and protecting household possessions and other key assets against theft,
Multiple exit routes/other way to go outside of the house in case of hazard (fire, flooding, earthquake)

Access and usability, including for persons facing mobility barriers (persons with physical, mental, and psychosocial disabilities)
nodes.question: How adequately do living spaces support privacy, domestic activities, interior climate, energy and fire safety, intrusion protection and accessibility—and where do habitability or dignity gaps most constrain household life?

nodes.name: Accessibility And Usability
nodes.definition: Whether households can enter, move through, and use rooms and fixtures when members face mobility, sensory, cognitive, or psychosocial barriers—ramps or level thresholds, door widths, reachable cooking and washing points, and layouts that do not exclude persons with disabilities from ordinary domestic routines.
nodes.question: Can persons with physical, mental, or psychosocial disabilities enter and use the dwelling’s rooms and fixtures without barriers?

nodes.name: Electricity Access And Supply
nodes.definition: Whether a dwelling has electrical connection inside or only outside the premises, how many hours per day power is available, and how reliable supply is for lighting and other household uses—separate from portable lamps or candles counted as non-food items.
nodes.question: Is electricity available inside or near the dwelling, and for how many hours per day is supply reliable?

nodes.name: Indoor Fire And Egress Safety
nodes.definition: Indoor fire-risk conditions around cooking and heating—non-flammable stove bases, safe distance between fuel stores and heat sources, and other practices that reduce ignition—and whether occupants have more than one workable way out during fire, flooding, earthquake, or similar hazards.
nodes.question: Are cooking and fuel-storage practices fire-safe, and can occupants exit safely if fire, flood, or earthquake occurs?

nodes.name: Interior Climate And Habitability
nodes.definition: Interior conditions that make daily life livable: ventilation that clears humidity, condensation, and smoke from cooking, heating, or lighting; heating or cooling when needed; safe and affordable energy for thermal comfort and lighting; adequate floor-to-ceiling height; disease-vector measures such as long-lasting insecticide-treated nets; and culturally appropriate interior arrangements for family life.
nodes.question: Are ventilation, thermal comfort, ceiling height, vector protection, and cultural fit of the interior adequate for daily domestic life?

nodes.name: Intrusion And Asset Protection
nodes.definition: Ability to lock or otherwise secure doors and openings against unauthorized entry, and to keep household possessions and other key assets safe from theft when the dwelling is occupied or left unattended.
nodes.question: Can households lock the shelter and protect possessions against intrusion and theft?

nodes.name: Privacy And Living Space
nodes.definition: Floor area and internal layout for family life relative to household size—people per room, separated rooms or partitions, a workable place for food preparation (separate room, veranda, communal or open-air cooking), and enough space for sleeping and private activity without severe overcrowding.
nodes.question: Is subdivided space for family life, cooking, and sleeping sufficient relative to household size and people per room?

nodes.name: Dwelling envelope
nodes.definition:
Information related to:

The type of dwelling (tent, building, single family house, semidetached house, apartment building (loft, studio, etc.), collective center, tents/makeshift, homeless on the street, etc. 
The kind of materials the building/structure is made of (vernacular local building materials, cement/concrete materials, etc.), and the durability of the dwelling, 
The overall state of the structure/building (unfinished building, precarious/sub-standard, etc.).
The state of the structure/enclosure/envelope (foundation, beams, columns, walls, floor roof, window, door, insulation layers, etc.). Observational component to determine structural safety are: tilting of columns, beams, doors, balconies, or stairs, bowing or bulging walls, visible cracks in stairs, walls, columns, lintels or beams, bowing or sagging in the roof, sagging in the floor, broken doors, cracks in windows, etc.
The degree of functioning of the enclosure (walls, doors, windows, roof),
The degree of protection given by the shelter in relation to rain and leakages, direct sunlight/radiant heat, cold, heat, wind, dust, damp, moisture or mold, noise, rodents and insects, fumes, and smell from other shelters. 
The presence of dangerous materials/parts, e.g., cutting edges, falling material, broken glasses.
nodes.question: What dwelling types, materials and structural conditions are people occupying, how well do roofs, walls, floors and openings protect against weather, pests and injury hazards, and where is enclosure failure most severe?

nodes.name: Building Materials And Durability
nodes.definition: What walls, roof, floor, and frame are made of—vernacular local materials, cement or concrete, timber, metal sheets, tarpaulin, or mixed scrap—and whether those materials hold up under local climate and the length of time households are expected to stay.
nodes.question: What materials predominate in current shelters, and are they durable enough for local climate and expected occupancy?

nodes.name: Dwelling Types Occupied
nodes.definition: Forms of shelter households actually occupy: tents or makeshift structures, unfinished or precarious buildings, single-family or semi-detached houses, apartments, collective centres, or sleeping outdoors—and how those forms relate to household needs and options in the area.
nodes.question: What dwelling forms are households occupying, and do available types meet needs across location and displacement status?

nodes.name: Enclosure Element Functioning
nodes.definition: How well the shelter enclosure works in practice—whether walls, doors, windows, and roofs close, open, seal, and stay in place as intended, including missing panes, jammed or broken doors, gaps in walls, and roofs that no longer enclose living space.
nodes.question: Do walls, doors, windows, and roofs still operate and enclose living space as intended?

nodes.name: Moisture Damp And Mold Conditions
nodes.definition: Dampness, rain ingress, condensation, and mold or fungal growth on or inside the envelope—leaking roofs and walls that leave interiors wet, degrade finishes, and worsen indoor air quality.
nodes.question: Where and how often do shelters show damp, leakage, or mold that harms interior conditions?

nodes.name: Structural Condition And Safety
nodes.definition: Overall state of the building or structure—unfinished, precarious, or sub-standard—and observable defects in foundation, beams, columns, walls, floors, roof, openings, and insulation layers, such as tilting members, bowing or bulging walls, cracks in stairs or lintels, sagging roofs or floors, and broken openings that signal structural risk.
nodes.question: What share of shelters show tilting, cracking, sagging, or other defects that compromise structural safety?

nodes.name: Weather Pest And Injury Hazards
nodes.definition: How far the envelope shields occupants from rain, wind, dust, sun and radiant heat, cold or heat, noise, rodents and insects, and fumes or smells from neighbouring shelters, plus injury risks from sharp edges, falling debris, broken glass, or other dangerous parts.
nodes.question: How well do shelters block weather, pests, and noise, and where do hazardous parts put occupants at injury risk?

nodes.name: HLP
nodes.definition:
Information related to the relationship and issues among groups or individuals with respect to housing, land, and properties, established through statutory law or customary, informal, or religious arrangements. It includes the way in which House/Land/Property is held, used, and transferred among individuals or entities, and the associated rights, responsibilities, and obligations that come with it. It encompasses:

The tenure system (who can use what resources, for how long, and under what conditions).

The tenure arrangement, ranging from full ownership and formal rental agreements to emergency housing, informal settlement, and occupation of land (e.g., own property right, renting contract, shelter granted with permission by organizations/authorities/ relatives/family/community, accommodation without formal ownership, lease and/or use agreements, squat without permission, owner without property title, renter without rental contract, tenure system of camp, etc.)

The systems, institutions, rules, and processes that oversee and regulate HLP tenure, and transfer or inheritance of HLP from one owner to another. It may include laws, policies, regulations, and dispute resolution mechanisms.
nodes.question: How secure and documented are housing, land and property tenure arrangements, how well do governance, dispute resolution and transfer systems function, and where do unclear rights or weak formalization most put households at risk?

nodes.name: Dispute Incidence And Resolution Access
nodes.definition: Conflicts among neighbours, relatives, hosts, or other community actors over who may hold or use housing, land, or property, and whether parties can reach and use formal courts, customary forums, or other legal and quasi-legal pathways when those disputes arise.
nodes.question: Where do housing and land disputes among community members occur, and can affected parties access workable resolution mechanisms?

nodes.name: HLP Governance And Regulation
nodes.definition: Institutions, laws, policies, and administrative rules that oversee housing, land, and property tenure—who may use what, for how long, and under what conditions—and how those frameworks operate for crisis-affected populations in practice.
nodes.question: Which policies and institutions regulate HLP for the affected population, and how functional are they on the ground?

nodes.name: Ownership Clarity And Documentation
nodes.definition: How clearly claims to housing, land, or property are identified and evidenced—titles, deeds, customary recognition, rental contracts, or other proof—and where ambiguous, contested, or missing paperwork leaves rights uncertain.
nodes.question: How clearly can households demonstrate ownership or use rights, and where is documentation missing or contested?

nodes.name: Rights Awareness And Obligations
nodes.definition: How well households and other actors understand the rights, duties, and responsibilities that come with holding, using, or transferring housing, land, and property under statutory, customary, informal, or religious systems.
nodes.question: How well do households understand their HLP rights and obligations under the systems that apply to them?

nodes.name: Tenure Arrangements And Security
nodes.definition: How households hold and use shelter or land—full ownership, formal or informal rental, hosted or permitted use, camp tenure, squatting, or occupation without permission—and how secure those arrangements are, including eviction and forced-displacement risk for informal settlers and undocumented occupants.
nodes.question: What tenure arrangements do households hold, and how exposed are informal settlers to eviction or forced relocation?

nodes.name: Transfer Inheritance And Formalization
nodes.definition: How housing, land, and property pass between people through sale, gift, or inheritance, and practical barriers when registration, titles, or other formal documentation needed for lawful transfer is incomplete, lost, or unavailable.
nodes.question: How are transfers and inheritance carried out in practice, and what missing documentation blocks formalization?

nodes.name: Non-food household items
nodes.definition:
Information related with the non-food domestic assets, such as:

Sleeping, blanket and bedding (floor mat, mattress, sheeting), 
Other furniture (table, chairs, etc.)
Assets to prevent hypothermia or heat strokes, 
Lightning
Personal clothing, sets of clothing per person, size and type appropriate to culture, season, and climate, and adapted to particular needs,
Tools and fixing: necessary tools, fixing, and complementary training for the maintenance or construction for shelter (nails, wire, rope, etc.).
nodes.question: How available and adequate are bedding, furniture, lighting, clothing, thermal-protection assets and shelter tools for households, and which NFI gaps most undermine comfort, safety or shelter maintenance?

nodes.name: Domestic Lighting Items
nodes.definition: Portable or stand-alone lighting solutions households use for evening and off-grid activity—lamps, torches, candles, fuel, batteries, or solar lights—and whether those devices give enough light for safe domestic routines, distinct from grid electricity supply.
nodes.question: What lighting solutions do households rely on, and is light adequate for safe evening domestic activity?

nodes.name: Household Furniture
nodes.definition: Basic furniture for daily living—tables, chairs, storage pieces, and comparable items that allow sitting, eating, studying, and ordinary household functioning—and gaps when such furnishings are missing or shared beyond usable capacity.
nodes.question: Which essential furniture for daily living do households have, and where do gaps block ordinary domestic functioning?

nodes.name: Personal Clothing
nodes.definition: Clothing sets available per person—quantity, size, and type suited to culture, season, and climate, and adapted for particular needs such as disability, pregnancy, or age—so people can dress with dignity in current conditions.
nodes.question: Do household members have enough culturally and seasonally appropriate clothing for current conditions?

nodes.name: Shelter Tools And Fixings
nodes.definition: Tools, fixings, and complementary skills or training needed to maintain, repair, or build shelter—hammers, nails, wire, rope, and related materials—so households can keep structures usable.
nodes.question: What tools, fixings, and related know-how do households have for shelter repair or construction?

nodes.name: Sleeping And Bedding Items
nodes.definition: Sleeping and bedding materials—blankets, floor mats, mattresses, sheeting, and related coverings—and whether stocks are adequate for household size, climate, and rest without sharing beyond workable limits.
nodes.question: Are sleeping and bedding materials sufficient for household size and climate?

nodes.name: Thermal Protection Assets
nodes.definition: Portable or household assets that help occupants avoid hypothermia or heat stroke beyond the building fabric itself—extra coverings, insulating materials, fans, or other climate-response items suited to cold snaps or heat waves.
nodes.question: What household assets help people cope with extreme cold or heat, and how sufficient are they under current conditions?

nodes.name: Settlement
nodes.definition:
Information related to the different scenarios of settlement, such as:

For non-displaced population: 

Owner occupying accommodation or land (houses, apartment, land),
Rental accommodation or land,
Informally occupied accommodation or land (empty houses, apartments, vacant land).

For displaced populations: 

Dispersed: 
Rental arrangement (renting accommodation, renter status), e.g., houses, apartments, land from existing housing stock,
Hosted arrangement (hosted by host population), e.g., houses, apartments, land already occupied or made available by the host population.
Spontaneous arrangement (self-settle accommodation, informal settler status), e.g., empty houses, empty apartments, vacant land, road side,

Communal : 
Collective accommodation/collective center. Pre-existing facility or structure where multiple households take shelter, e.g., public buildings, evacuation, reception and transit centers, abandoned buildings, company compounds, unfinished buildings,
Planned settlement/planned camp. A purpose-built settlement for displaced people, e.g., formal settlements managed by government, UN, NGOs, or civil society. Can include transit or reception centers or evacuation sites,
Unplanned settlement. Multiple households spontaneously and collectively settle in a location, creating a new settlement, e.g., informal sites and self-settlements.

Additional characteristics of settlement scenarios:

Geographic context, urbans, peri urban, rural,
Settlement density (overcrowding, etc.),
Duration/phase, temporary, permanent, short term, medium term, long term,
Site management, managed, remote or mobile managed, self-managed, no management,
Unsafe or insecure settlement environments, areas with known natural or man-made threats, risks and hazards related to local geography, climate, public health, or social/political context,
Security on the way to/from the settlement,
Distance and time between the settlement and services/facilities/installations,
Place for social facilities culturally acceptable, place for culturally appropriate burial, place for livestock accommodation,
Usable surface/people, population density in the settlement
nodes.question: In which settlement scenarios—displaced or non-displaced, dispersed or communal—are people living, how do density, duration, site management, security and service reach shape conditions, and where are settlement risks or access gaps most acute?

nodes.name: Communal Settlement Arrangements
nodes.definition: Multi-household settlement forms for displaced people—collective centres in pre-existing facilities, purpose-built planned camps, and spontaneous or unplanned sites where many households settle together—and the shared-living and coordination pressures that arise at those scales.
nodes.question: What communal forms are in use, including spontaneous or unplanned sites, and what shared-living challenges affect residents at scale?

nodes.name: Displaced Dispersed Settlement
nodes.definition: Dispersed settlement of displaced households through rental of existing housing stock, hosting by local households, or spontaneous self-settlement in empty dwellings, vacant land, or roadside locations—outside purpose-built camps or collective centres.
nodes.question: Among displaced households in dispersed settings, what share are renting, hosted, or spontaneously self-settled, and under what conditions?

nodes.name: Non-Displaced Settlement Scenarios
nodes.definition: How non-displaced households are housed—owner-occupied dwellings or land, rental of housing or land, or informal occupation of empty houses, apartments, or vacant land—and whether that housing is adequate relative to household needs across urban, peri-urban, and rural areas.
nodes.question: How are non-displaced households settled—owner occupancy, rental, or informal occupation—and is housing adequate across areas?

nodes.name: Service Reach And Social Facilities
nodes.definition: Distance and travel time from settlements to essential services, facilities, and installations, and whether sites include culturally acceptable space for social facilities, burial, and livestock accommodation.
nodes.question: How far are settlements from essential services, and do sites provide culturally appropriate space for social facilities, burial, and livestock?

nodes.name: Settlement Density And Duration
nodes.definition: Geographic context (urban, peri-urban, rural), population density and overcrowding, usable surface relative to people, and the planned or actual duration and phase of settlement—temporary, short-, medium-, or long-term, or permanent—including whether time horizons are defined for temporary sites.
nodes.question: How do density, overcrowding, and defined settlement duration or phase shape living conditions at current sites?

nodes.name: Site Management And Security
nodes.definition: Site management arrangements (managed, remote or mobile managed, self-managed, or unmanaged), unsafe or insecure settlement environments with known natural or man-made threats tied to geography, climate, public health, or social and political context, and security along routes to and from the site.
nodes.question: How are sites managed, and what unsafe or insecure conditions affect residents inside the settlement and along access routes?

nodes.name: WASH
nodes.definition: Information related to water, sanitation and hygiene conditions that protect public health and dignity in households, communities and institutions. It covers water supply quantity and safety; excreta management across the sanitation chain; hygiene facilities and products; solid waste management; vector control; and WASH standards in health care facilities and schools. It is used to classify content on environmental health risks and the adequacy of WASH services and practices.
nodes.question: How adequate and safe are water supply, sanitation, hygiene, solid waste and vector-control arrangements—including WASH in health facilities and schools—and where do service or practice gaps most expose people to contamination and disease risk?

nodes.name: Excreta management /sanitation
nodes.definition: Information related to the entire sanitation service chain (from the toilet via collection and conveyance to the final treatment and safe disposal and/or reuse), to safely contained excreta to avoid contamination of the natural, living, learning, working and communal environments. It encompasses all the steps in which sanitation products such as human excreta, urine, faeces, dry cleansing materials, anal cleansing water, flushwater, blackwater, menstrual hygiene products are managed from the point of generation to the point of use or ultimate disposal, the user safety at the point of use and the use, by all, of sanitation facilities at all times. It also refers to the routine operation and maintenance (O&M) of toilets which include all activities needed to run a sanitation scheme.
nodes.question: How well does the full sanitation chain—from toilet access and containment through collection, conveyance, treatment and disposal or reuse—protect people and environments from excreta-related contamination, and where do access, O&M or service gaps leave the greatest risk?

nodes.name: Collection and Conveyance Systems
nodes.definition: Information related to sewers, vacuum trucks, emptiers, pipes and other physical arrangements that move human excreta, urine, faeces, flushwater, blackwater, dry cleansing materials, anal cleansing water and menstrual hygiene waste from toilets and households toward treatment or disposal points along the sanitation service chain.
nodes.question: What collection and conveyance options move sanitation products from toilets onward, and where do broken pipes, missing emptiers or interrupted trucking cut the chain?

nodes.name: Containment and Environmental Contamination Risk
nodes.definition: Information related to whether pits, septic tanks and other containment keep excreta sealed through the service chain, and to overflows, leaks, open emptying or dumping that drive faecal contamination of living, learning, working and communal environments and of nearby water sources.
nodes.question: Where is containment failing through leaks, overflows or open emptying, and which living areas or water points show faecal contamination as a result?

nodes.name: Facility Upkeep and Hygienic Condition
nodes.definition: Information related to routine cleaning, repair and continuous operation of toilets and sanitation schemes—including desludging schedules, spare parts and caretaker arrangements—and to the resulting hygienic or unhygienic state users encounter at the facility.
nodes.question: How regularly are toilets cleaned, repaired and desludged, and what unhygienic conditions currently deter use or endanger users?

nodes.name: Sanitation Practices and Service Monitoring
nodes.definition: Information related to community awareness and education on safe sanitation practices—including toilet use, hand hygiene after defecation and avoidance of open defecation—and to feedback, inspections or monitoring data used to judge whether the sanitation service chain is performing as intended.
nodes.question: What sanitation messages reach communities and what practices are adopted, and what monitoring evidence shows whether the service chain is working?

nodes.name: Toilet Access Safety and Inclusion
nodes.definition: Information related to whether women, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable groups can physically reach and use toilets at all times, and to user safety measures at facilities—lighting, locks, privacy screens, gender-separated stalls and protection from harassment—that enable dignified use rather than open defecation.
nodes.question: Which women, children and persons with disabilities can safely reach toilets day and night, and what lighting, locks or privacy gaps still push people to defecate in the open?

nodes.name: Treatment Disposal and Reuse Outcomes
nodes.definition: Information related to final treatment plants, burial, controlled dumping or reuse of faecal sludge, blackwater and menstrual hygiene waste, and whether end-of-chain practice prevents pollution of natural and communal environments.
nodes.question: How are sludge and menstrual hygiene waste finally treated, buried, dumped or reused, and does that practice stop environmental pollution?

nodes.name: Hygiene facilities and products
nodes.definition: Information related to the facilities necessary to perform personal hygiene to maintain the cleanliness of the body and clothing and preserve the overall health and wellbeing. It includes the safe usage of showers/bathing, handwashing facilities and laundry areas and the behaviours related to safe wastewater management and needed to ensure that the facilities do not become a breeding site for vectors. It also refers to the routine operation and maintenance (O&M) of hygiene facilities which include all activities needed to run a facility scheme. Hygiene products refers to soap for laundry and personal hygiene; washable/disposable sanitary napkins for women; underwear for women, men (and children as appropriate); washable diapers for babies; bedpans for young children; toilet bowls/urinals/pierced chairs for people with disabilities; anal cleansing containers; razor blades, nail clippers, combs, shampoo; toothbrushes and toothpaste; treated mosquito nets and ORS sachets and items needed for the O&M activities of hygiene facilities as bleach, mop, bucket, brush, broom, etc.
nodes.question: To what extent can people access and safely use bathing, handwashing and laundry facilities and essential hygiene products, and how do O&M, wastewater/vector risks and hygiene practices affect whether facilities remain usable and protective?

nodes.name: Essential Hygiene Product Availability
nodes.definition: Information related to whether households and individuals can obtain soap for laundry and bathing, washable or disposable sanitary napkins, underwear, washable baby diapers, bedpans, adaptive toilet aids, anal cleansing containers, razors, nail clippers, combs, shampoo, toothbrushes and toothpaste, treated mosquito nets and ORS sachets needed for personal hygiene and wellbeing.
nodes.question: Which soap, menstrual materials, diapers, nets, ORS and adaptive aids can different groups obtain, and where are the sharpest supply shortfalls?

nodes.name: Facility Upkeep and Operating Supplies
nodes.definition: Information related to routine operation and maintenance of showers, handwashing points and laundry areas, and to stocks of bleach, mops, buckets, brushes, brooms and other consumables needed to keep those facilities functional and clean.
nodes.question: Who cleans and repairs hygiene facilities, and are bleach, mops, buckets and brushes available in enough quantity?

nodes.name: Facility Wastewater and Vector Risk
nodes.definition: Information related to drainage and handling of greywater from bathing, handwashing and laundry areas, and to stagnant pools or blocked drains that could turn hygiene facilities into breeding sites for mosquitoes and other disease vectors.
nodes.question: How is wastewater from bathing and laundry drained or contained, and do stagnant conditions create mosquito or other vector breeding sites?

nodes.name: Hygiene Practices Knowledge and Social Norms
nodes.l3: Hygiene Practices Knowledge and Social Norms
nodes.definition: Information related to community awareness of personal hygiene practices—handwashing with soap, bathing, laundry and menstrual hygiene—and to sociocultural norms, beliefs or barriers that encourage or constrain those daily behaviours.
nodes.question: What do people understand about personal hygiene practices such as handwashing and menstrual care, and which social norms support or block them?

nodes.name: Personal Hygiene Facility Access
nodes.definition: Information related to the presence, reach, privacy and usable design of showers, bathing spaces, handwashing stations and laundry areas needed for body and clothing cleanliness, including ramps, seating and other adaptations that allow persons with disabilities to use them safely.
nodes.question: Which bathing, handwashing and laundry facilities can people actually use, and how accessible and private are they for persons with disabilities and women?

nodes.name: Solid waste management
nodes.definition: Information related to the process of generation to collection, transport, treatment, and disposal of solid waste to avoid pollution of the natural, living, learning, working and communal environments. It also includes all behaviours which ensure that solid waste is safely contained, collected and potentially treated at households’ level to ensure a clean and safe household and community environment.
nodes.question: How is solid waste generated, contained, collected, treated and disposed of from households through communal systems, and where do service gaps, unsafe practices or pollution expose people and environments to the greatest harm?

nodes.name: Collection and Transport Services
nodes.definition: Information related to the regularity, coverage and modalities of collecting and hauling solid waste from households and communal areas—door-to-door pickup, communal bins, skip trucks or informal collectors—toward treatment or disposal points.
nodes.question: How frequently and widely is solid waste collected and hauled, and where does uncollected refuse pile up in streets or yards?

nodes.name: Community Engagement and Waste Practices
nodes.definition: Information related to public awareness of safe solid waste handling—segregation, storage and disposal—and to community roles, clean-up campaigns and shared neighbourhood arrangements that keep household and communal environments clean.
nodes.question: What do residents know about safe waste handling, and how do communities organise participation or clean-ups that keep neighbourhoods free of refuse?

nodes.name: Environmental Pollution and Health Exposure
nodes.definition: Information related to pollution of natural, living, learning, working and communal environments by unmanaged dumps, burning or litter, and to health hazards for people living near dumpsites, scavenging waste or encountering contaminated ground and air.
nodes.question: Where is unmanaged waste polluting living or natural environments, and what health exposures affect people near dumps or who handle refuse?

nodes.name: Treatment Infrastructure and Disposal Practice
nodes.definition: Information related to facilities and methods used to treat, recycle, bury, burn or finally place solid waste, and to whether open dumping, uncontrolled burning or burial practices are controlled enough to avoid environmental pollution.
nodes.question: What treatment, recycling or final placement options exist, and how controlled are dumping, burning or burial practices?

nodes.name: Waste Generation and Household Containment
nodes.definition: Information related to the types and volumes of solid waste produced at household and community level, and to household behaviours that keep waste segregated, bagged or bin-stored and ready for collection so homes and compounds stay clean and safe.
nodes.question: What waste streams and volumes are generated, and how do households contain, segregate and prepare refuse for collection?

nodes.name: Vector control
nodes.definition: Information related to the presence of breeding and feeding sites of potential vectors of communicable diseases and the measures required to prevent them and protect individuals from significant risks to health and well-being. Vectors include: mosquitoes, fleas, lice, rodents, snakes, ticks and sandflies.
nodes.question: Where and why are disease vectors proliferating, what environmental, community and individual control measures and programme capacity are in place, and how adequate are surveillance and care access for vector-borne illness risks?

nodes.name: Care Access for Vector-Borne Illness
nodes.definition: Information related to whether people with malaria, dengue, cholera-linked diarrhoeal disease or other vector-borne illness can reach diagnosis, treatment and referral services when symptoms appear.
nodes.question: Can people with suspected malaria, dengue or similar illness reach timely diagnosis and treatment, and what barriers delay care?

nodes.name: Control Programme Resources and Capacity
nodes.definition: Information related to staffing, spray equipment, larvicide and insecticide stocks, nets, funding and organisational capacity available to plan and sustain vector control measures against mosquitoes, fleas, lice, rodents, snakes, ticks and sandflies.
nodes.question: What human, material and financial resources back vector control measures, and where do capacity shortfalls limit spraying, larviciding or net distribution?

nodes.name: Environmental and Community Control Measures
nodes.definition: Information related to environmental and community vector control measures—source reduction, drainage of standing water, residual spraying, larviciding, rodent proofing and clean-up campaigns—intended to interrupt breeding and feeding near populations, and to public awareness of vector-related health risks that motivates participation.
nodes.question: Which drainage, spraying, larviciding or clean-up actions are underway, and do communities understand the health risks enough to sustain participation?

nodes.name: Habitat Conditions and Proliferation Drivers
nodes.definition: Information related to breeding and resting sites of mosquitoes, fleas, lice, rodents, snakes, ticks and sandflies, and to environmental, seasonal and climate-change drivers—flooding, drought, warming or altered rainfall—that shift vector distribution and favour proliferation.
nodes.question: Where are breeding and resting habitats concentrated, and how are seasonal shifts or climate change altering vector distribution?

nodes.name: Individual Protection Measures
nodes.definition: Information related to personal and household means of reducing contact with disease vectors—insecticide-treated nets, window screens, repellents, protective clothing and sleeping practices—and to whether people know when and how to use them against mosquitoes, fleas, lice, ticks and sandflies.
nodes.question: Which nets, screens, repellents and protective behaviours can people obtain and correctly use, and how adequately do they cut exposure?

nodes.name: Vector Population Surveillance
nodes.definition: Information related to monitoring of vector density, species composition and geographic distribution over time—including larval surveys, trap catches and early-warning signals—used to guide control interventions.
nodes.question: How are mosquito and other vector populations sampled and tracked, and what do recent findings show about density and risk trends?

nodes.name: WASH in health care facilities
nodes.definition:
Information related to all measures required to maintain minimum WASH infection prevention and control standards. It includes:

The water scheme established and its operation and maintenance to ensure sufficient quantity of safe water to the patients, visitors and staffs;

The excreta management scheme and its operation and maintenance to safely contain excreta/vomits to avoid contamination of the working and surroundings environments. It encompasses from the point of generation to the point of use or ultimate disposal and the user safety;

The hygiene facilities as functioning hand washing facilities, showers and laundries 

The solid waste management system including the segregation of waste at the collection points until the final disposal

The cleaning of and hygiene measures in the infrastructures and environments

Standard Precautions (the minimum infection prevention practices that apply to all patient care, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status of the patient, in any setting where healthcare is delivered)

Dead body management in case of outbreak
nodes.question: Do health care facilities meet minimum WASH and IPC standards across water supply, excreta containment, hygiene stations, healthcare waste, cleaning/standard precautions and outbreak body handling, and where are the most critical infection-prevention gaps?

nodes.name: Cleaning Standard Precautions and IPC
nodes.definition: Information related to cleaning and hygiene measures in health care infrastructures and environments—wards, theatres, toilets and waiting areas—and to consistent application of Standard Precautions, the minimum infection prevention practices applied to all patient care regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status.
nodes.question: How consistently are facility cleaning routines and Standard Precautions applied across care areas, and where do hygiene gaps undermine infection prevention?

nodes.name: Facility Excreta Containment Chain
nodes.definition: Information related to toilets, sluices and sanitation schemes in health care settings that safely contain excreta and vomit from generation through conveyance to treatment or disposal, including user safety for patients and staff and protection of working and surrounding environments from faecal contamination.
nodes.question: How are excreta and vomit contained from generation to disposal inside facilities, and where could leaks contaminate wards, grounds or surroundings?

nodes.name: Facility Hygiene Stations and Laundry
nodes.definition: Information related to functioning handwashing points with soap and water, showers and laundry arrangements in health care facilities required for infection prevention and for hygiene of patients, visitors and staff.
nodes.question: Are handwashing stations, showers and laundries functional at points of care, and can staff and patients use them whenever needed?

nodes.name: Facility Water Supply and Reliability
nodes.definition: Information related to the water scheme serving health care facilities—quantity, safety and continuity for patients, visitors and staff—and to operation and maintenance that keep pumps, tanks, pipes and treatment reliable day to day.
nodes.question: Do facilities deliver enough safe water for patients, visitors and staff, and how reliable is day-to-day operation and maintenance of the water scheme?

nodes.name: Healthcare Waste Segregation and Disposal
nodes.definition: Information related to segregation of infectious, sharps, pharmaceutical and general healthcare waste at collection points inside facilities, and to safe transfer through to incineration, autoclaving or other final treatment or disposal without exposing staff, patients or the environment.
nodes.question: How is healthcare waste segregated at collection points and disposed of, and where do gaps create infection or environmental risks?

nodes.name: Outbreak Mortuary and Body Handling Protocols
nodes.l3: Outbreak Mortuary and Body Handling Protocols
nodes.definition: Information related to written procedures, personal protective equipment, mortuary space and practised arrangements for managing dead bodies in health care facilities during outbreaks, as part of minimum WASH infection prevention and control standards.
nodes.question: What outbreak-ready body-handling protocols, PPE and mortuary arrangements exist in facilities, and how adequately do they limit transmission?

nodes.name: WASH in schools
nodes.definition:
Information related to all measures required to maintain a healthy and dignified learning environment.

The water scheme established and its operation and maintenance to ensure sufficient quantity of safe water to the students and staffs;

The excreta management scheme and its operation and maintenance to safely contain excreta to avoid contamination of the learning and surroundings environments. It encompasses from the point of generation to the point of use or ultimate disposal and the user safety;

The hygiene facilities as functioning hand washing facilities

The hygiene behaviours at school

The solid waste management system 

The cleaning of and hygiene measures in the infrastructures and environments
nodes.question: How adequate and reliable are school water, sanitation, handwashing, solid waste and cleaning arrangements, and how do student and staff hygiene practices support a healthy and dignified learning environment?

nodes.name: School Cleaning and Environmental Hygiene
nodes.definition: Information related to cleaning routines and hygiene measures applied to classrooms, toilets, yards, kitchens and other school infrastructures and environments needed to keep a healthy and dignified learning setting.
nodes.question: What cleaning schedules and hygiene measures are applied across school buildings and grounds, and how adequate are they to keep learning spaces healthy?

nodes.name: School Handwashing Facility Functionality
nodes.definition: Information related to the presence, location, soap and water availability, and day-to-day functionality of handwashing facilities that students and staff need throughout the school day.
nodes.question: Are handwashing facilities with soap and water functional where students and staff need them, and can they be used throughout the school day?

nodes.name: School Sanitation Containment and Safety
nodes.definition: Information related to school toilets and excreta management from generation through conveyance to disposal or reuse, including gender-separated stalls, locks, lighting and other user-safety features, and prevention of faecal contamination of learning spaces and surroundings.
nodes.question: How are school toilets containing excreta through to disposal, and where do safety gaps or contamination threaten the learning environment?

nodes.name: School Solid Waste Handling
nodes.definition: Information related to collection, storage, segregation and disposal of solid waste generated on school grounds—classroom litter, canteen waste and sanitary waste—as part of keeping a healthy learning environment.
nodes.question: How is solid waste collected, stored and disposed of within schools, and does practice keep classrooms and grounds free of refuse?

nodes.name: School Water Supply and Reliability
nodes.definition: Information related to the water scheme serving schools—sufficient quantity and safety for drinking and domestic needs of students and staff—and to operation and maintenance of pumps, tanks, taps and treatment that keep water available during the school day.
nodes.question: Do schools provide enough safe drinking and domestic water for students and staff, and how reliable is operation and maintenance of school water systems?

nodes.name: Student and Staff Hygiene Practices
nodes.definition: Information related to hygiene behaviours practised by students and staff at school—handwashing after toilet use and before eating, menstrual hygiene management, and food-handling hygiene—and to how consistently those behaviours are taught and applied.
nodes.question: What hygiene behaviours do students and staff actually practise at school—including handwashing and menstrual care—and how consistently are they applied?

nodes.name: Water supply
nodes.definition: Information related to the measures necessary to provide sufficient quantities of safe water to meet the drinking and domestic needs, without causing a risk to health. It encompasses all the steps from source exploitation, intake, abstraction and treatment to distribution methods, the user safety at the point of use and the behaviours related to safe water management and needed to ensure that the clean water provided remains uncontaminated until the point of use.
nodes.question: How sufficient, continuous and safe is water from source through treatment and distribution to household use, and where do quantity shortfalls, quality risks or unsafe handling most undermine drinking and domestic needs?

nodes.name: Drinking Water Quantity and Household Access
nodes.l3: Drinking Water Quantity and Household Access
nodes.definition: Information related to whether populations can obtain sufficient volumes of water for drinking and domestic needs without health risk, including distance to points, waiting times, rationing and service coverage across households and sites.
nodes.question: Can households obtain enough water for drinking and domestic use, and where do distance, queues or rationing create the sharpest shortfalls?

nodes.name: Point-of-Use Safety and Handling Practices
nodes.definition: Information related to whether water remains uncontaminated between delivery and consumption, and to household and community storage, handling and hygiene practices—covered containers, clean ladles, household treatment and knowledge of safe water management—that prevent recontamination at the point of use.
nodes.question: How do households store and handle water before drinking, and what do communities know about keeping water safe until the point of consumption?

nodes.name: Source Availability Yield and Seasonality
nodes.definition: Information related to exploitation, intake and abstraction from wells, boreholes, springs, rivers, rainwater and other sources used for drinking and domestic needs—including yield and accessibility—and to seasonal variations and climatic swings that reduce availability or dry sources at parts of the year.
nodes.question: Which sources supply drinking and domestic water, and how do dry-season or other seasonal variations cut yield and access?

nodes.name: Source Water Quality and Protection
nodes.definition: Information related to microbiological and chemical quality of water at the source, and to protective measures or contamination pathways—open defecation near intakes, livestock access, industrial discharge or damaged wellheads—that determine whether abstracted water is safe.
nodes.question: What is the microbiological and chemical quality at source, and which contamination pathways or protection gaps put that quality at risk?

nodes.name: Treatment and Distribution Continuity
nodes.definition: Information related to treatment processes after abstraction and to water-supply infrastructure and distribution methods—piped networks, trucking, standpipes, kiosks and storage tanks—that determine whether safe water reaches users continuously and equitably, including failures in those distribution methods that produce scarcity.
nodes.question: What treatment works and distribution infrastructure move water to users, and where do network breakdowns, trucking gaps or inequitable standpipe access create scarcity?
